screens.title: Deploying React dApps to IPFS and Arweave
screens.subtitle: Make your frontend as decentralized as your smart contracts

narration.text: In this lesson you'll learn how hosting your React dApp on decentralized storage preserves accessibility and resists censorship. We'll explain how IPFS uses content-addressing to identify files by a cryptographic hash, what pinning services like Pinata or Infura do, and why Arweave can provide permanent one-time-paid storage. You will also see a practical deployment flow: build the React app, use a pinning service SDK to upload the build folder, and then open your app via a public gateway. For example, after running a deploy script with Pinata you receive a CID you can paste into a gateway URL to load the site. We'll compare trade-offs: IPFS is efficient for mutable workflows and cheaper pinning, while Arweave trades a one-time fee for permanent storage. A common pitfall to watch for is forgetting to build the app or missing the homepage setting, which breaks client-side routing when users open deep links. By the end you should be able to pin your build folder, confirm a CID, and choose the right storage strategy for your dApp. Ready to explore the steps and code?

keyIdea.title: Core idea
keyIdea.text: Decentralize the frontend by publishing built static files to content-addressed storage so your dApp stays available and verifiable even if centralized hosts fail.

narration.text: By the end of these screens you will be able to identify the weaknesses of centralized hosting for dApps and the protections decentralized storage offers. You will understand IPFS's content-addressed model and how a CID guarantees immutability and verifiability of static frontend files. You will learn how to use a pinning service such as Pinata or Infura to pin your React build folder and retrieve a CID, and you will know how to access your dApp through a public gateway. Finally, you'll be able to compare IPFS and Arweave and pick the right solution for either frequent updates or permanent archival storage. For example, you'll recognize when to run a simple pinning script versus paying Arweave for one-time permanent storage. These skills let you keep your application's frontend accessible even when centralized providers fail, and they reduce the risk that a functioning smart contract becomes unreachable due to hosting choices.

screens.title: Why centralized hosting breaks dApp availability
screens.subtitle: Single points of failure and censorship risk explained

narration.text: A functioning smart contract on the blockchain is only part of a usable dApp; the frontend must also be reachable. Centralized hosting such as an S3 bucket or Netlify introduces a single point of failure: if that server or service is down, your dApp's UI becomes inaccessible even though the contract continues to operate. Centralized hosts are also subject to takedown or censorship, which contradicts the Web3 goal of decentralization. Consider a wallet or token sale: the contract still holds funds and rules, but users cannot interact with it if the UI is offline. A concrete example is deploying a React app to a cloud provider and relying on that provider's uptime. If the provider experiences an outage, users cannot perform ordinary actions. The misconception is thinking that because smart contracts live on-chain, the frontend doesn't matter; in reality the frontend is the most common usability barrier. The key takeaway is simple: decentralize your static frontend files so they are served from a distributed network and survive single-node failures. Ask yourself: if one host goes down, can a user still load my dApp and complete the same interactions?

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Centralized hosting creates single points of failure; decentralizing static assets helps maintain availability and resist censorship.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.2 › Why centralized hosting breaks dApp availability
Core Concept

Single point failures and censorship

Even with decentralized contracts, a centralized frontend can make the dApp effectively offline. This undermines decentralization goals.

Key points
  • Centralized servers can go down or be removed by a provider.
  • Smart contracts remain on-chain, but users lose a usable interface.
  • Decentralized storage removes this single dependency and increases resilience.
Key Takeaway

Treat the frontend as part of the decentralized system. Hosting choices directly affect whether users can interact with your contracts.

Concrete scenario
A token sale front end goes offline while the smart contract still accepts transactions. Users cannot interact with the sale because the interface is unavailable, demonstrating the need to decentralize frontend hosting.
Common mistake
Assuming that on-chain code alone provides user access. Always verify frontend availability strategy when auditing dApp resilience.
Why this matters
Users judge dApps by how reliably they can interact with them. Decentralized storage improves trust and uptime.

screens.title: IPFS and Content Addressing
screens.subtitle: How CIDs make files immutable and verifiable

narration.text: IPFS is a peer-to-peer distributed file system that identifies files by content, not by server location. Content-addressing means a file is requested by its cryptographic hash, called a CID, so the address is intrinsically tied to the exact bytes of the content. This guarantees immutability: change a single byte and the CID changes. A useful concrete example is an index. html file in your React build. When you pin that file and its assets, each file receives a CID. The collection of files published under a single directory can be addressed by the root CID. A common misconception is to treat IPFS like a conventional URL host; unlike a domain-based URL, a CID points to content regardless of the node serving it, and gateways resolve CIDs into HTTP responses. Understand that IPFS does not automatically guarantee perpetual storage — nodes must host or pin content. This is where pinning services come in. The key takeaway: CIDs provide verifiability and tamper evidence, which makes frontends trustable by content integrity rather than server identity. How would you verify a file's integrity if you receive a CID from a third party?

keyIdea.title: IPFS core
keyIdea.text: IPFS uses content-addressing via CIDs, making files verifiable and immutable while relying on nodes to host those CIDs.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.2 › IPFS and Content Addressing
Definition

Content-addressing and CIDs

CIDs are cryptographic hashes of file content. They let anyone verify that the bytes they received match what the publisher intended.

What to remember
  • A CID identifies exact content; it is immutable.
  • Changing content changes the CID, so versions get different addresses.
  • Gateways translate CIDs into HTTP access for browsers.
Key Takeaway

Use CIDs to verify asset integrity and to reference immutable builds when you publish a dApp frontend.

Concrete example
Pinning the React build folder produces an IPFS root CID. That CID references the exact index.html and asset files the browser will load.
Common misconception
IPFS is not a permanent host by default: content must be kept by nodes. Pinning services provide persistent hosting guarantees at a cost.
Why it matters
Immutable CIDs increase trust: anyone can verify the build hasn’t been tampered with, which is critical for distributed applications.

screens.title: Build your React app for IPFS
screens.subtitle: Create a production-ready build folder and prepare assets

narration.text: The first practical step is creating a production build of your React dApp. Running the standard command, typically npm run build or yarn build, compiles your React components into a static build folder containing H T M L, C S S, JavaScript bundles, and asset files. These static files are what you will upload to IPFS or Arweave. After building, verify that the build folder contains an index. html and asset directories for JS and C S S. A common routing issue arises when using client-side routing libraries: assets may be referenced with absolute paths and cause 404s when loaded via a gateway. To avoid this, set the package. json homepage to a relative base such as "homepage": "." which tells the build tool to use relative asset paths. Always test the build locally by serving the build folder with a static server to ensure the app loads and routes correctly. Misconceptions include skipping the build step and attempting to pin source files; IPFS requires the static output. The practical takeaway: verify build contents, fix asset paths, and confirm the app works from the build folder before uploading to any pinning service.

keyIdea.title: Build step
keyIdea.text: Run a production build and verify relative asset paths to ensure client-side routing works when served from gateways.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.2 › Build your React app for IPFS
Process

Build steps

  1. Run npm run build or yarn build to produce a build/ folder.
  2. Confirm index.html and static asset directories exist inside build/.
  3. Set package.json homepage to "." when using client-side routing.
  4. Serve the build locally to test routes and assets before uploading.
Concrete check
Open index.html from the build folder on a static server. Navigate to a sub-route and refresh to ensure no 404s. If you see missing assets, check the homepage configuration.
Routing pitfall
Client-side routing expects index.html to be served for all paths. Without relative asset paths, gateways may try to fetch absolute paths that don't exist, causing 404s. The package.json homepage set to "." prevents this.
Key Takeaway

Always build and test the static output locally. Fix asset paths and routing before uploading to decentralized storage.

screens.title: Pinning Services vs Running Your Own Node
screens.subtitle: Trade-offs between convenience, reliability, and maintenance

narration.text: You have two common options for making files available on IPFS: run your own IPFS node or use a pinning service such as Pinata or Infura. Running your own node gives you full control over your content and avoids third-party trust, but you are responsible for uptime, storage costs, and ensuring that content stays pinned. A pinning service abstracts those concerns: they host robust nodes, manage persistence, and provide SDKs or web dashboards to upload directories. A concrete example: using Pinata you can authenticate with A P I keys, call their pinFromFS method to pin a build folder, and receive a CID without maintaining your own node. The misconception is to equate pinning services with permanence; pinning services guarantee availability while they continue to store the content, but they are still a hosted solution. For absolute permanence, consider using Arweave. The practical guidance is to use pinning services for convenience and development, run your own node if you need control, and plan for backups or archival to Arweave for critical assets. Which trade-offs align with your project's trust and uptime requirements?

keyIdea.title: Pin vs own node
keyIdea.text: Pinning services reduce maintenance overhead; running your own node increases control but increases operational responsibility.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.2 › Pinning Services vs Running Your Own Node
Pinning Service
Convenience & reliability
  • Managed nodes and guaranteed pinning while under service.
  • SDKs and dashboards for quick deployment.
  • Requires API key management and trust in provider.
Own Node
Control & maintenance
  • Full control and no third-party dependency.
  • Requires continuous operation and storage management.
  • Better for projects that demand trust minimization.
Concrete example
Use Pinata to upload build/ with pinFromFS and receive a CID, saving the overhead of running your own node during development and early production.
Common mistake
Assuming pinning services equal immutability forever. They maintain availability while pinning, but permanence requires a different model or Arweave's economic guarantee.
Key Takeaway

Pick pinning for ease of deployment and Arweave for permanent archival; running your own node is for projects that require full control.

screens.title: Deploy script with the Pinata SDK
screens.subtitle: A Node.js example to pin your React build folder

narration.text: This lesson walks through a canonical deploy script that uses the Pinata SDK to pin a built React app. The script authenticates with A P I keys from environment variables, points to the build directory, tests authentication, and calls pinFromFS to upload the directory and receive an IPFS hash. The concrete example below mirrors a real deployment: install @pinata/sdk and dotenv, add your A P I keys to a. env file, and adjust the buildFolderPath to your build output. A common mistake is committing A P I keys or forgetting to set them, so the script includes a guard that exits with an error if keys are missing. Another misconception is reading the IpfsHash as a mutable pointer; the returned hash is a CID representing that upload and should be shared as the permanent address for that pinned snapshot. After running the script you will see the CID printed and you can open it via a gateway to verify the site. Practice reading the output to confirm a successful pin and then test the URL in a browser. Deploy script with the Pinata SDK means authenticate with pinata, point to the build folder, and use pinfromfs to upload and retrieve the cid for public access.. In practical terms, a node.js example to pin your react build folder. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Deploy script idea
keyIdea.text: Authenticate with Pinata, point to the build folder, and use pinFromFS to upload and retrieve the CID for public access.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.2 › Deploy script with the Pinata SDK
Code
// scripts/deploy-ipfs.js
const pinataSDK = require('@pinata/sdk');
const fs = require('fs');
const path = require('path');
require('dotenv').config();

const pinataApiKey = process.env.PINATA_API_KEY;
const pinataSecretApiKey = process.env.PINATA_SECRET_API_KEY;
const buildFolderPath = path.resolve(__dirname, '../build'); // Path to your React build folder

if (!pinataApiKey || !pinataSecretApiKey) {
  console.error("PINATA_API_KEY and PINATA_SECRET_API_KEY must be set in your .env file.");
  process.exit(1);
}

const pinata = new pinataSDK({ pinataApiKey, pinataSecretApiKey });

async function deployToIpfs() {
  try {
    await pinata.testAuthentication();
    console.log("Pinata authentication successful.");

    const options = {
      pinataMetadata: { name: 'MyReactDApp' },
      pinataOptions: { cidVersion: 0 }
    };

    const result = await pinata.pinFromFS(buildFolderPath, options);
    console.log("DApp successfully pinned to IPFS!");
    console.log("IPFS CID:", result.IpfsHash);
    console.log("Access your dApp at: https://gateway.pinata.cloud/ipfs/" + result.IpfsHash);
  } catch (error) {
    console.error("Error deploying to IPFS:", error);
    process.exit(1);
  }
}

deployToIpfs();
Walkthrough
Install @pinata/sdk and dotenv, add API keys to .env, set the buildFolderPath, then run node scripts/deploy-ipfs.js after building. Check the terminal for the returned IpfsHash.
Common mistake
Committing API keys or leaving them undefined causes authentication to fail. Always keep keys in .env and out of source control.
Key Takeaway

The deploy script automates pinning; read the terminal output to retrieve and verify the CID that represents your build snapshot.

screens.title: Run the deployment and verify the CID
screens.subtitle: Terminal commands and what success looks like

narration.text: This lesson simulates the terminal steps you run during deployment and explains the typical outputs you should expect. First, ensure you are in the project root and have built the React app. Install dependencies with npm install @pinata/sdk dotenv if needed. Confirm your. env contains PINATA_API_KEY and PINATA_SECRET_API_KEY. Run node scripts/deploy-ipfs. js. A successful run prints a confirmation that authentication passed and logs an IpfsHash value — the CID — followed by one or more gateway URLs you can open in a browser to validate the site. For example, the script will print a gateway. pinata. cloud link with the CID appended. If you see errors, check for missing keys, incorrect buildFolderPath, or network issues. A common misconception is that a successful CID implies permanence; it means the content is pinned by that service, but long-term permanence depends on continued pinning or moving to Arweave. The practical step after receiving a CID is to open the gateway URL, navigate within the app, refresh deep routes, and confirm assets load. If a deep route 404s, revisit the homepage setting and rebuild.

keyIdea.title: Deployment verification
keyIdea.text: A printed IpfsHash confirms a successful pin. Always open the gateway URL and test navigation and asset loading to verify deployment.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.2 › Run the deployment and verify the CID
Terminal Demo
Commands
# Build your app and run the deploy script
npm run build
npm install @pinata/sdk dotenv
node scripts/deploy-ipfs.js
Expected output
  • Pinata authentication successful.
  • DApp successfully pinned to IPFS!
  • IPFS CID: Qm... or bafy... (a CID string you can paste into gateways)
Key Takeaway

Run, read the CID, and then validate by opening it in a gateway. Test deep routes and asset loading.

Common errors
Missing API keys, incorrect build path, or network timeouts are frequent. Check .env, paths, and try re-running the script after confirming build/ contents.
Pro tip
Keep a copy of the CID in project deployment notes and consider pinning to multiple services or archiving to Arweave for redundancy.

screens.title: Arweave: permanent storage versus pinning
screens.subtitle: When to prefer Arweave for dApp assets

narration.text: Arweave provides a different economic model: a one-time payment for permanent storage. Its blockweave design and incentive structure encourage nodes to store data indefinitely after upload. Practically this means that when permanence is critical—archival content, legal records, or immutable assets—you can pay once and rely on the network to keep the data without continuous pinning. A concrete example is publishing an official contract UI snapshot or immutable metadata you want to preserve permanently; paying Arweave may be appropriate. A common misconception is thinking Arweave replaces flexible updates; because uploads are permanent, updated versions produce new entries, and the previous snapshots remain accessible. For dApps that require frequent updates, IPFS with pinning services is more cost-effective and flexible. Many teams combine approaches: pin frequently updated assets on IPFS and archive critical releases to Arweave. The takeaway is to match your storage choice to how often assets change and how much permanence you require. Arweave: permanent storage versus pinning means arweave offers permanent, one-time-paid storage; use it when immutability and perpetual availability are essential.. In practical terms, when to prefer arweave for dapp assets. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Arweave summary
keyIdea.text: Arweave offers permanent, one-time-paid storage; use it when immutability and perpetual availability are essential.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.2 › Arweave: permanent storage versus pinning
Definition

Permanent storage model

Arweave charges a one-time fee to store data permanently. This suits archives and assets that must remain unchanged and available forever.

Considerations
  • Pay once for archival permanence.
  • Uploads are immutable snapshots; updates create new data entries.
  • Best for regulatory archives, historical records, and high-value immutable assets.
Key Takeaway

Use Arweave when you need a permanent, paid guarantee that your dApp assets will remain available indefinitely.

Concrete example
Archive a release binary or signed UI snapshot to Arweave when you need to ensure it will never be altered or removed.
Misconception
Arweave is not a convenience replacement for frequent updates; because stored data is permanent, you will create new uploads for each version.

screens.title: Public gateways and client routing
screens.subtitle: How gateways let browsers access IPFS content and routing fixes to avoid 404s

narration.text: Browsers cannot speak IPFS natively, so public gateways act as HTTP bridges that resolve CIDs and return normal web responses. After you pin a build folder and get a CID, the gateway URL looks like a regular HTTP address with the CID appended. When users access that URL, the gateway fetches the content and serves it like any web server. This makes IPFS content accessible to standard browsers without special plugins. However, client-side routing needs careful handling: if a user opens a subpath directly, the gateway tries to fetch that file path from the CID and will return 404 if it doesn't exist. The fix is to build with relative asset paths by setting the homepage field to "." in package. json, so the index. html becomes the entry point for all routes and react-router can handle navigation. A common misconception is that gateways will automatically rewrite routes; they will not. The practical step is to test deep links on the gateway after deployment and adjust the build configuration if you see missing assets or 404 pages. This ensures reliable navigation for end users.

keyIdea.title: Gateways and routing
keyIdea.text: Public gateways bridge IPFS to browsers; ensure relative asset paths and index-based routing to avoid 404s on subpaths.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.2 › Public gateways and client routing
Architecture

Gateway bridge

Gateways translate HTTP requests into IPFS content resolution by CID so browsers can load files without native IPFS support.

Checklist to prevent 404s
  • Add "homepage": "." to package.json when using react-router.
  • Build and verify index.html exists in build/.
  • Open the gateway URL with a subpath to test deep-route behavior.
Key Takeaway

Gateways enable browser access but do not rewrite routes; build with relative paths and test deep links after deployment.

Concrete test
Open https://gateway.pinata.cloud/ipfs/<CID>/dashboard and refresh. If you see index.html content and react-router renders the page, routing is configured correctly.
Common misconception
Believing gateways will automatically serve index.html for all paths; adjust build settings instead.

screens.title: Hands-on: deploy a built React dApp to IPFS using Pinata
screens.subtitle: Step-by-step lab checklist from build to verification

narration.text: Follow this hands-on checklist to deploy your built React dApp to IPFS using Pinata. Start by confirming a working React build: run npm run build and verify the build/ folder contains index. html and static assets. Next, sign up for Pinata and obtain an A P I key and secret. In your deployment project create a. env file with PINATA_API_KEY and PINATA_SECRET_API_KEY and install @pinata/sdk and dotenv. Adjust the buildFolderPath in the deploy script to point to your build folder. Run node scripts/deploy-ipfs. js. On success the script returns an IpfsHash CID. Copy the CID into a public gateway URL and open it in a browser to confirm the site loads and navigation works. If a route 404s, set "homepage": "." in package. json, rebuild, and re-run the deploy to obtain a new CID. A common error is forgetting to test authentication; the script includes testAuthentication to catch invalid keys early. This hands-on sequence ensures repeatable deployments and helps you troubleshoot common failures. Hands-on: deploy a built React dApp to IPFS using Pinata means build, secure api keys in .env, run the pinning script, fetch the cid, and validate the gateway url and routes.. In practical terms, step-by-step lab checklist from build to verification. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Lab checklist
keyIdea.text: Build, secure API keys in .env, run the pinning script, fetch the CID, and validate the gateway URL and routes.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.2 › Hands-on: deploy to IPFS
Hands-on Activity

Deployment checklist

  1. Run npm run build and verify build/ has index.html and static assets.
  2. Create a Pinata account and get API key and secret.
  3. Add keys to a .env file and install @pinata/sdk dotenv.
  4. Set correct buildFolderPath in scripts/deploy-ipfs.js and run the script.
  5. Copy returned CID into a gateway URL and validate the live dApp, including deep routes.
Key Takeaway

Follow the checklist and re-run builds when fixing routing or asset path issues to ensure the CID reflects the corrected snapshot.

Concrete note
After each meaningful change, rebuild and repin to publish the new snapshot under a new CID. Keep records of CIDs for releases.
Common mistake
Uploading source files instead of the build output is incorrect; only static built files will render correctly in browsers via gateways.

screens.title: Common mistakes and quick fixes
screens.subtitle: Verify build, check API keys, and fix routing issues

narration.text: When deployments fail or users see intermittent availability, a short checklist will resolve most problems. First, verify you ran the build step; missing build artifacts is the most common cause of empty or broken pages. Second, ensure A P I keys for Pinata or Infura are set in a. env file and are not committed to source control. If the deploy script errors, confirm testAuthentication in the SDK returned success. Third, test the CID via multiple public gateways; intermittent unavailability may be due to gateway issues rather than your pinned content. Fourth, fix routing by adding "homepage": "." to package. json and rebuilding so asset URLs are relative. Misconceptions include assuming a single successful pin guarantees global availability: gateways or network partitions may still cause temporary access problems. The final suggestion is to maintain deployment logs with CIDs and consider archiving critical snapshots to Arweave for permanent storage. These quick checks will dramatically reduce common deployment failures. Common mistakes and quick fixes means confirm build artifacts, secure api keys, test authentication, verify gateway access, and fix routing with a homepage setting.. In practical terms, verify build, check api keys, and fix routing issues. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Troubleshooting checklist
keyIdea.text: Confirm build artifacts, secure API keys, test authentication, verify gateway access, and fix routing with a homepage setting.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.2 › Common mistakes and quick fixes
Troubleshooting

Quick fixes

  • Build artifacts missing? Run npm run build and re-deploy.
  • Authentication failing? Check .env and API keys for typos and permissions.
  • Intermittent availability? Try another gateway and confirm the pin is intact.
  • Routing 404s? Add "homepage": "." to package.json, rebuild, and repin.
Key Takeaway

A short checklist resolves most deployment problems: build, authenticate, repin, and test across gateways.

Pro tip
Keep a small deployment log recording the CID and build commit hash so you can correlate user reports to the exact snapshot deployed.
Assessment idea
Simulate a broken route and fix it with the homepage change, rebuild, repin, and verify that the CID now serves working navigation.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.subtitle: What to remember from this chapter

narration.text: These three concepts will guide your deployment decisions. First, decentralized storage means storing files across many nodes rather than on a single server, increasing censorship resistance and availability. Second, IPFS uses content-addressing with CIDs so any file can be verified by its hash; use pinning services to keep content available. Third, pinning services like Pinata or Infura provide reliable hosting for IPFS content by running long-lived nodes and exposing gateways. Remember to build your React app, secure A P I keys, set relative asset paths if using client-side routing, and always verify the returned CID by opening it in a gateway. These principles help ensure users can interact with your dApp regardless of centralized hosting outages. Verify builds

Record CIDs
